story: Over the last two million years glaciers have repeatedly covered Fiordland, grinding hard rock — gneiss, diorite and granite — into U-shaped valleys that are now lakes and fiords. Fourteen fiords, some reaching 40 kilometres inland, run from Milford Sound/Piopiotahi in the north to Preservation Inlet in the south. Milford Sound is 16 kilometres long and 265 metres deep in places. Inland, hundreds of lakes dot the land; Lake Hauroko, at 462 metres, is the deepest in New Zealand.

Rain shapes everything. Up to seven metres a year falls around Milford Sound, and it lays a permanent layer of fresh water, stained the colour of tea by the forest, over the sea in the fiords; beneath it a band of unusual marine life clings to the rock walls. East of the mountains the land is drier, and the Eglinton Valley is red beech forest, home to mohua/yellowhead, kākāriki and long-tailed bats, which DOC protects with intensive pest control. Kea haunt the Homer Tunnel, and rare rock wrens live among its boulders.

Māori knew Fiordland well, and their traditions tell how Tuterakiwhanoa carved its landscape from formless rock. Few lived here year-round, but seasonal camps were linked by well-worn trails, and translucent takiwai greenstone was sought near the mouth of Piopiotahi — named for the piopio, a native thrush now probably extinct. One inland route crossed what is now the Milford Track, over Omanui/McKinnon Pass and down to Lake Te Anau. Captain Cook spent five weeks in Tamatea/Dusky Sound in 1773, and sealers and whalers followed his charts.

Donald Sutherland built three huts at Milford in 1878 and called them the City of Milford. Quintin McKinnon and Ernest Mitchell found the pass that bears McKinnon's name in 1888, and the Milford Track was opened and guided from 1889. Gold brought a brief boom to Preservation Inlet in the 1890s, while Richard Henry moved kākāpō and kiwi to islands in Dusky Sound. Work on the Homer Tunnel began in 1935 and was finished in 1954. The national park was constituted in 1952 and declared a World Heritage Area in 1986.
howItWorks: Fiordland is public conservation land managed by the Department of Conservation (DOC), and there is no entry fee: the National Parks Act gives the public freedom of entry and access. That may change for overseas visitors at Milford Sound. The Government is investigating an access levy for international visitors at four sites, Piopiotahi/Milford Sound among them; the Conservation Amendment Bill that would allow it was introduced on 7 May 2026. Nothing is charged until it becomes law and regulations follow — check before you go.

Three of DOC's Great Walks are here. The Milford Track is walked one way over three nights, by boat from Te Anau Downs and back from Sandfly Point, with no camping; the Kepler is a loop from Te Anau; the Routeburn ends at The Divide on the Milford Road. In the Great Walks season — 1 November to 30 April, from 27 October on the Kepler — huts and campsites must be booked well ahead, and international visitors pay more than New Zealanders. The huts have mattresses, heating, basic cooking and a resident ranger. Out of season, facilities are cut back and the tracks need alpine, river-crossing and navigation skills.

Milford Sound is reached by the Milford Road (part of SH94), by air, or at the end of the Milford Track. Doubtful Sound has no road: tours cross Lake Manapōuri by boat to West Arm and take a coach over Wilmot Pass to Deep Cove. Avalanches usually fall between May and November; check the New Zealand Avalanche Advisory before going high. Dogs and other pets are not allowed in the park, and flying a drone needs a DOC permit.

sightNotes.poi-nz-fiordland-milford-sound-piopiotah: The fiord at the end of the Milford Road, 16 km long and up to 265 m deep. Cruises leave from the visitor terminal; a marine reserve protects its waters.
sightNotes.poi-nz-fiordland-mitre-peak: Sheer rock walls rising 1,692 metres straight from the water, one of the world's most photographed peaks. The Milford Sound Foreshore Walk has some of the best views.
sightNotes.poi-nz-fiordland-sutherland-falls: Falls dropping 580 metres in three leaps from Lake Quill, a side trip of 1 hr 30 min return on the third day of the Milford Track, below Omanui/McKinnon Pass.
sightNotes.poi-nz-fiordland-mirror-lakes: Small lakes beside the Milford Road, about 56 km from Te Anau, reflecting the Earl Mountains. A 10-minute wheelchair-accessible stroll.
sightNotes.poi-nz-fiordland-key-summit: A side trip from the Routeburn Track near The Divide to an alpine wetland, with views of the Darran Mountains and Hollyford Valley; 1–1.5 hours return.
sightNotes.poi-nz-fiordland-lake-marian: An alpine lake in a glacier-carved hanging valley, 1.5 hours up a steep track off Hollyford Road; waterfalls 10 minutes in. Keep off the lake edge in winter and spring.
sightNotes.poi-nz-fiordland-homer-tunnel: The Milford Road's tunnel, begun in 1935 and finished in 1954. Traffic signals can hold you up to 20 minutes; kea are often seen here.
sightNotes.poi-nz-fiordland-doubtful-sound-patea: A large, remote fiord with three main arms and no road, home to one of the southernmost bottlenose dolphin populations. Reached by boat and coach via Lake Manapōuri.
sightNotes.poi-nz-fiordland-mount-luxmore: The highest point of the Kepler Track at 1,472 metres, a 30-minute side trip from the ridge, with views over Lake Te Anau's South Fiord to the Murchison Mountains.
sightNotes.poi-nz-fiordland-lake-hauroko: New Zealand's deepest lake, 462 metres, in the south of the park, reached by road off the Southern Scenic Route; boats can be launched here.

entrances: Te Anau, the gateway town, with the visitor centre and the Kepler Track; Te Anau Downs for the Milford Track boat
The Milford Road (SH94), 119 km from Te Anau to Milford Sound/Piopiotahi, with The Divide (Routeburn Track) and Hollyford Road on the way
Manapōuri, 21 km from Te Anau, for boats to West Arm and Doubtful Sound
The Southern Scenic Route to Lake Monowai, Lake Hauroko and Tuatapere in the south
planYourVisit.reservations: Milford, Kepler and Routeburn Track huts and campsites must be booked for the Great Walks season, and Luxmore Hut on the Kepler needs a booking all year; bookings are open for 2026/27. Doubtful Sound trips are booked with transport operators, and Milford Road campsites should be booked online before you go. The international visitor access levy proposed for Milford Sound is not yet law — check with DOC before you go.
permits: Flying a drone needs a DOC permit
Taking a vehicle over the Wilmot Pass Road to Doubtful Sound needs a permit, and the road carries a charge
Hunting on conservation land needs a DOC hunting permit
camping: DOC campsites along the Milford Road between Te Anau and The Divide; book online
Freedom camping is not allowed within 200 metres of the Milford Road
Great Walk campsites on the Kepler and Routeburn tracks; no camping on the Milford Track, and no overnight stays in the Kepler's day shelters
lodging: Hotels, motels and campgrounds in Te Anau and Manapōuri; limited facilities at Milford Sound
Great Walk huts on the Milford, Kepler and Routeburn tracks
Backcountry huts throughout the park, paid with hut tickets or a Backcountry Hut Pass
seasonalClosures: The Milford Road can close for weather, rockfall, snow and avalanches; from May to September snow chains may be required — check the road status before you go
No stopping between the Hollyford Road junction and The Chasm, an avalanche zone
Great Walk facilities are greatly reduced from May to October, and the tracks need alpine skills

chronology.text: Captain James Cook spends five weeks in Tamatea/Dusky Sound; New Zealand's position is fixed at Astronomer's Point.
Donald Sutherland builds three thatched huts at Milford Sound, the 'City of Milford'.
Quintin McKinnon and Ernest Mitchell find the route over Omanui/McKinnon Pass.
McKinnon and Sutherland open the Milford Track and begin guiding tourists; William Homer finds the saddle later named after him.
Gold brings a brief boom to Preservation Inlet; Richard Henry begins moving kākāpō and kiwi to islands in Dusky Sound.
Work begins on the Homer Tunnel; delayed by hard conditions and the Second World War, it is finished in 1954.
Fiordland is declared a World Heritage Area; in 1990 it becomes part of Te Wāhipounamu – South West New Zealand.
The Conservation Amendment Bill, which would allow an access charge for international visitors at Milford Sound, is introduced on 7 May.

safety: If an earthquake at Milford Sound is long or strong, drop, cover and hold, then move uphill and away from the water at once: a landslide could set off a tsunami in the fiord.
Drive the Milford Road with care: it is narrow, winding and alpine. Never stop in the avalanche zone between the Hollyford Road junction and The Chasm, and in winter know how to fit chains.
Outside the Great Walks season the Milford, Kepler and Routeburn tracks cross avalanche terrain; check the New Zealand Avalanche Advisory and the Avalanche Terrain Exposure Scale before you go.
Gertrude Saddle and other alpine routes become treacherous in rain, snow or ice; if there is rain or snow, do not go.
regulations: No dogs or other pets in Fiordland National Park.
Flying a drone without a DOC permit is prohibited.
No freedom camping within 200 metres of the Milford Road, and no discharging waste along the road or anywhere in the park.
Check, clean and dry all gear between waterways; watercraft may not enter Lake Manapōuri's tributary rivers, because of didymo.
Do not feed kea or other wildlife.

weather: Fiordland's weather is highly changeable: cold, snow, strong winds and heavy rain can come in any month, though it can be sunny too, and up to seven metres of rain falls a year around Milford Sound. The Great Walks season, from late October or November to April, is the best time to tramp; it is also when the Milford Road is busiest, especially from 9.30 am to 1.30 pm. Alpine flowers bloom around the Homer Tunnel in summer once the snow clears. From May to September the road can be icy and snowbound, and avalanches usually fall between May and November. Lake Manapōuri often turns rough in the afternoons.
directions: Te Anau is reached on SH6 and SH94 from Queenstown, 179 km and about 2 hours 20 minutes, or on SH1 and SH94 from Invercargill, 150 km and about 2 hours; regular buses run from both. From Te Anau the Milford Road takes about 2.5 hours without stops, and from Queenstown about 4.5 hours; allow more than journey planners suggest, and fill up in Te Anau, as there is no fuel on the way. Coaches run to Milford Sound, and there are airports at Te Anau, Manapōuri and Milford Sound.
